paras: The attempted lynching of George Wells took place at Elyria, Ohio, on May 10, 1882, when fellow workmen and neighbors gathered to lynch Wells, a young man just arrested on a charge of raping a girl. Officers got Wells away from the crowd and he was jailed, and at his trial later that month he was acquitted. None of the reports gives the race of anyone involved.

According to an Elyria dispatch printed in the Wheeling Register, at about nine o'clock on the evening of Sunday, May 7, Eva Broughton, a girl of about sixteen who lived on Lake avenue, was attacked and raped while walking home alone from church at the avenue's crossing of the Tuscarawas Valley and Wheeling Railway. She reached home, described her assailant, and afterward was said to be in a critical condition.

On May 10 George Wells, an employee of the Elyria Screw and Tap Company, was arrested "on suspicion" and taken by officers to the girl's house, where she identified him. Word of the identification spread, and some of Wells's fellow workmen and some neighbors gathered about the house "with the purpose of lynching him on the spot." The Elyria dispatch says the officers "managed to elude them", while a brief in the Eaton Democrat says the officers stopped the lynching by drawing their revolvers on the mob.
Wells was then brought before Squire Doolittle, waived examination, and was sent to jail because he could not post bail.

The Elyria column of the Wellington Enterprise reported on May 17 that the case, brought "at the instance of Miss Boughton," would be heard the next day, and that "great interest" was felt because both parties were well known. A week later the same column reported that Wells had been tried on Tuesday and "honorably acquitted." No report of arrests among the crowd appears in the coverage.

The Wheeling Register ran the story on May 12 under the headline "OUTRAGED. An Attempt to Lynch a Villain Frustrated by the Police," calling the assailant a "dastardly villain" and judging it "extremely probable" that Wells was guilty. The same dispatch promised that "there will be no lynching" but said Wells would "receive no mercy from the court or jury." The Eaton Democrat gave the case one paragraph among its Ohio state news on May 18, spelling the name "Welles."

The Wellington Enterprise, published in the same county, mentioned only the hearing and the acquittal, in single lines of its Elyria column, and said nothing of the mob. None of the papers that presumed Wells guilty is shown reporting his acquittal.

The accounts differ on how the officers kept Wells from the crowd: the dated Elyria dispatch says they eluded it, while the unattributed Eaton Democrat brief says they drew revolvers. They also differ on the girl's age, about sixteen in the Wheeling Register and seventeen in the Eaton Democrat.

bases: Workmen and neighbors gathered to lynch the arrested man, and officers got him away from them (A1, A4); no paper gives anyone's race, so whether this was anti-Black violence is not shown.
A crowd gathered to lynch Wells over an alleged rape (A1, A4), but officers kept him from it and he was later acquitted (A5); nobody was killed, so this was an attempted lynching.

The Wheeling Register's Elyria dispatch (A1) and the Eaton Democrat's state brief (A4) both report the arrest and a mob held off by officers, and the Wellington Enterprise's local column confirms the charge and the trial (A2, A5); the two accounts differ on how the officers did it.

George Wells ('Welles' in the Eaton Democrat), a young man employed by the Elyria Screw and Tap Company; race not stated.
Accused of raping Eva Broughton ('Miss Boughton'), aged about sixteen or seventeen, as she walked home from church.
Some of Wells's fellow workmen and some neighbors ('the mob').
